JSON: Name: ceeci_gfz_sbm_malmquist Title: Unexpected-output SBM-DEA combined with Malmquist index for city-level evolution analysis of carbon emission efficiency in the construction industry Short Hypothesis: Increases in technical progress (as measured by the Malmquist technological change index) cause increases in total factor productivity of carbon emission efficiency (TFP>1) of the construction industry at the city level over 2013–2022. Related Work: Existing approaches measure carbon emission efficiency either as single-factor indicators (carbon intensity, carbon productivity) or as total-factor efficiency using frontier methods. Two main families of methods are common: parametric stochastic frontier analysis (SFA) and nonparametric data envelopment analysis (DEA). DEA variants used in the literature include CCR/BCC radial models, three-stage DEA (DEA+SFA adjustment), super-efficiency SBM, and SBM extensions that treat CO2 as an undesirable output. For dynamics, the Malmquist (and Malmquist–Luenberger) index applied within DEA is the standard tool to decompose TFP into efficiency change and technological change. Limitations across prior work are: (1) most studies operate at provincial/national scale rather than at city granularity, (2) many DEA applications ignore undesirable outputs or use radial measures that mask slack behavior, (3) life-cycle embodied emissions are often omitted from DEA inputs/outputs, (4) dynamic analyses often stop at aggregate Malmquist scores without decomposing scale vs pure technical effects or classifying cyclical evolution modes, (5) small sample sizes, outliers, and panel imbalance produce sensitivity and reduce robustness, and (6) spatial dependence and policy shocks are frequently not integrated into the efficiency evolution analysis. Abstract: This project addresses city-level evolution of carbon emission efficiency in the construction industry by integrating an unexpected-output slack-based measure (SBM) DEA with Malmquist productivity decomposition. The study constructs a city-panel input–output dataset for a 16-city coastal agglomeration (2013–2022) using capital, labor, machinery and energy inputs, desired output (gross construction output) and undesirable output (CO2 emissions, including direct and upstream where available). We will compute static SBM efficiency scores, decompose Malmquist total factor productivity into efficiency change, technological change, pure technical change and scale change, and derive spatial-temporal typologies and cyclical evolution modes. The main contributions are: (1) city-level decomposition of drivers of CEECI, (2) quantification of the relative contribution of technological progress versus scale and managerial improvements, and (3) an empirical classification of evolutionary modes to inform differentiated policy measures. Expected outcomes are robust, mapped spatio-temporal patterns of CEECI, statistical estimates of driver contributions, and sensitivity-tested typologies for targeted regional policy design. Experiments: Datasets: assemble a balanced panel for 16 GFZ-CUA cities (Shantou, Jieyang, Chaozhou, Meizhou, Fuzhou, Quanzhou, Xiamen, Putian, Zhangzhou, Sanming, Nanping, Ningde, Longyan, Wenzhou, Lishui, Quzhou) for years 2013–2022. Variables: inputs = fixed asset investment (deflated to constant 2020 CNY), average annual number of construction employees, total year-end power of owned construction machinery (kWh) and annual construction-sector final energy consumption converted to standard coal equivalent; desirable output = nominal gross output of construction (deflated); undesirable output = CO2 emissions computed from sector energy consumption using standard emission factors and, where data permit, input–output based upstream emissions. Preprocessing: deflate monetary series to 2020, impute missing yearly city values using year-adjacent weighted interpolation, winsorize extreme values at 1st/99th percentiles for robustness checks. Primary methods and baselines: (A) unexpected-output SBM-DEA (VRS) as primary model; (B) baseline 1: radial CCR/BCC DEA without undesirable outputs; (C) baseline 2: super-efficiency SBM with undesirable outputs; (D) baseline 3: three-stage DEA (SFA-adjusted inputs) then SBM; (E) baseline 4: Malmquist index computed from standard DEA without undesirable outputs; (F) parametric comparison: panel SFA estimating CO2-constrained output frontier. Malmquist decomposition: compute TFP, EC, TC, PEC, SEC annually per city. Evaluation metrics: city-level SBM efficiency scores and bootstrapped 95% CIs (Nboot=1000), mean and variance of TFP and decomposed indices, paired Wilcoxon tests comparing primary model to baselines (alpha=0.05), spatial statistics: global Moran's I and local LISA for efficiency and TC, clustering stability: adjusted Rand index across classification thresholds. Ablation studies: (1) remove undesirable output (CO2) from model; (2) replace life-cycle CO2 with direct-combustion-only CO2; (3) omit machinery input; (4) change returns-to-scale assumption CRS vs VRS; (5) apply winsorization vs raw data; (6) compute bootstrap confidence intervals vs no bootstrap. Causal test: panel regression where annual city TFP (dependent) is regressed on lagged TC, controlling for city fixed effects and time effects; test hypothesis coefficient on lagged TC>0 (cluster-robust SEs). Implementation: use established DEA/SBM implementations (R packages or MATLAB), Malmquist computations per standard DEA distance functions, spatial analysis in R or ArcGIS. Reporting: present maps, time series per city, decomposition tables, bootstrap CIs, test statistics and p-values, and sensitivity tables from ablations. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data quality and coverage: city-level inputs (machinery power, life-cycle upstream emissions) may be missing or estimated, producing imputation bias; panel imbalance reduces Malmquist reliability. DEA sensitivity: SBM-DEA is nonparametric and sensitive to outliers and small sample sizes (n=16), which can inflate frontier influence and yield unstable efficiency scores. Identification and causality: Malmquist TC and panel regressions capture association but cannot prove causal mechanisms; endogeneity from concurrent policy shocks and economic cycles may confound TC→TFP inference. Measurement error: CO2 emission estimates based on energy consumption and regional factors may misstate undesirable output; omission of embodied emissions or differences in emission factors across cities limits comparability. Spatial dependence and spillovers: failure to explicitly model spatial spillovers in the primary DEA/Malmquist computations may bias city-level attributions. Scalability and generalization: results calibrated on one coastal agglomeration may not generalize to other regions or time windows. Computational limits: bootstrap and multiple ablation scenarios increase compute time but are tractable for this panel size; however, expanding to finer spatial/temporal granularity may require greater computational resources. Methodological limits: DEA-based Malmquist assumes comparable DMUs and balanced panels; violating these assumptions undermines index interpretation.
